shotSpec.capture: first viewport, scripts/take-route-shots.mjs default, scale 1, palette-quantized

defects.section: top of list / above the fold
defects.finding: The layout lock calls for a shadcn-command A-Z jump, but nothing in the first viewport offers any way to jump, filter, sort, or search the 47 subdivisions — no visible control of any kind exists before the row list starts. The page is a plain HTML list, not an adaptation of the demo.

All 47 rows repeat the identical shape (thumbnail or navy monogram, name, one-line description, a single gray progress bar, a count) with no hover state, expansion, or variation caught in the shots — it reads as a static table wearing one bar chart column rather than an interactive ledger.

On mobile the description text wraps to two lines on some rows (e.g. 'Deschutes River Recreation Homesites') and one line on others, so the bar/count baseline shifts row to row and the hairline rhythm breaks down the list instead of staying level.

rows.dullest: The row list itself: 47 near-identical rows (thumbnail or navy-monogram placeholder, name, one-line stat sentence, a plain gray bar, a count) with no map, no photo variety for the majority of rows, and nothing that responds to a cursor — it is a spreadsheet with one decorative bar column, not a directory built to be explored.
rows.beats: No win named
rows.verdict: This is a correct, on-brand list of subdivisions with real live counts and median prices, but it is not the shadcn-command A-Z directory the layout lock specifies — demoMatch is false because no jump, filter, or search control appears anywhere in the fold, and nothing else in the shot suggests one exists off-screen. Every row is the same inert shape repeated 47 times with a single gray bar as the only visual encoding, so interaction and originality score low even though typography and brand consistency (navy/cream/Amboqia/Geist) are intact. Fix by building the actual shadcn Command demo into the header (A-Z jump, live filter-as-you-type) and giving rows a reason to be touched, not just read.

tells: "Cream box" — the Tour/Call/Text control on mobile is three separate bordered buttons (one filled navy, two ghost outlines) with visible gaps between them, not the shadcn Button Group / beUI Action-swap single grouped control the catalog specifies for this exact job.

defects.section: Tour/Call/Text action row (mobile footer, desktop under price)
defects.finding: Three discrete buttons with a filled navy Tour and two outlined ghost buttons for Call/Text, exactly the leftover-ghost-button pattern the brief bans. No shared container, no single sliding/active-state control — it reads as three unrelated CTAs, not one grouped ask.

defects.section: Photo filmstrip under the hero (desktop) / thumbnail strip + arrow pair (mobile)
defects.finding: The hero media control is a static row of small square thumbnails with a caption chip ("1/35", "35 photos"), not a swipeable rail with the shadcn carousel's prev/next affordance and card motion. On mobile the round arrow buttons sit disconnected above the strip rather than embedded in the demo's own control, so it reads as a photo strip wearing a carousel's function, not the object itself.

defects.section: Price/specs block and "Talk to a broker" sidebar (desktop, left column and right rail)
defects.finding: Price, cut badge, and the bd/ba/sqft line are a stacked plain-text block with no visual encoding of the price cut over time or how this list price compares to the street/neighborhood; the broker card is a static bordered rectangle with a headshot and phone number, indistinguishable from any MLS syndication template. Nothing here rewards a hover or invites a second look.

rows.dullest: The price/specs stack on the left and the broker contact card on the right are both static, left-aligned text blocks — the same shape a Zillow or MLS syndication page uses. There is no chart of the $50K cut against days on market, no comp context, nothing that turns the numbers into a story; it is data placed on the page, not designed.
rows.beats: Zillow's own listing page — this page wins on directness: a named principal broker (Matt Ryan, photo, direct cell, "same-day reply" promise) replaces Zillow's rotating anonymous-agent-farm CTA. It does not win on media interaction, comp context, or visual originality — Zillow's carousel and gallery lightbox are more functional than this static filmstrip.
rows.verdict: This is a correct, on-brand, and functional listing page — full-bleed hero restored, real price-cut data, a direct broker ask — but it is the generic MLS-syndication template with Ryan Realty's navy and cream painted over it, not a page that would make someone stop scrolling. demoMatch is false: the Tour/Call/Text row is the exact three-ghost-button pattern the catalog brief calls out as a cream box rather than a grouped control, and the photo filmstrip is a static thumbnail strip standing in for the shadcn carousel's swipe interaction. Nothing here is originality-scored above a template; the fix is installing the two named catalog controls as the actual interactive objects, then giving the specs/price block a visual encoding instead of a stacked text list.

tells: "Scrolling lists as the design" — the entire comparison body below the photo row is a plain table wearing hairlines: label column, four value columns, thin dividers, no chart, no bar, no map.

Cream box / missing carousel — the photo strip per slot is one static exterior photo with no arrows, dots, or thumbnail strip. shadcn's Carousel demo is not present; this is a `` in a card, not the catalog interaction.

defects.finding: Each home shows exactly one static photo with no carousel controls (arrows, dots, swipe affordance) and no second angle — this is the 'Carousel import ≠ photo strip' cream-box case named in the brief, not the shadcn Carousel demo adapted into V3Carousel.

The table has no sort, no hover-row highlight, no winner-marking, and no visible affordance that it does anything beyond display static text; the partial-width underlines under some numeric cells (e.g. $1,050,000 gets a short underline while the lower $575,000 gets a longer one, and $269 price/sqft is only partially underlined despite being the lowest) don't track any consistent rule, reading as a rendering artifact rather than a real value encoding.

At 375px the second home column is cut off mid-address at the viewport edge with no fade, arrow, or dot indicator signaling more columns exist off-screen — a visitor has no cue to scroll horizontally.

rows.dullest: The feature comparison table itself — rows of Price, Price/sqft, Beds, Baths, Sqft, Lot, Year built as plain text with hairline dividers. It is accurate and on-brand but functionally identical to any portal's static spec sheet; nothing rewards a hover, tap, or scrub with more information.
rows.beats: No win named — this reads as a slightly better-typeset version of Zillow's or Redfin's own compare tool, not a page that beats it. No visible interactivity, no photo carousel, and no data encoding give it an edge over the portals it's implicitly competing with.
rows.verdict: This is a correct, on-brand, static feature table dressed in the house serif and navy/cream palette — it avoids the empty-slots trap (good) and cites its MLS source with a timestamp (good), but demoMatch is false: the photo strip has no carousel interaction at all, and the table shows no sort, highlight, or hover behavior that would make it the shadcn Table demo rather than a plain HTML table wearing hairlines. Ship this as the finished comparison and a visitor sees a spec sheet, not a tool worth returning to.

tells: "KPI grids" — seen in the navy stat bar: three numbers (1,529 / $749,500 / 30 days) separated by dots with no bar, sparkline, or mark encoding any of them, only a trailing plain-language clause

defects.section: photo strip below the stat bar
defects.finding: The layout lock calls for Field — a field of live homes via an inventory rail — directly under the Stage hero, but the first viewport shows a single static exterior photo with no carousel controls, no second/third home, no arrows, no dots, and no visible interaction of any kind.

Three figures sit in a flat horizontal row with no visual encoding — no sparkline, no bar, no trend mark — just bold numbers and dot separators; it reads as a KPI grid softened by prose rather than a data section that rewards a hover or scrub.

Nothing in either screenshot shows a hover state, cursor affordance, toggle, or scrubber — the 'Search homes' button and the photo are both inert; a visitor has zero reason to touch anything before scrolling.

rows.dullest: The photo strip under the stat bar — one static exterior shot of a home with no caption, no price, no way to see another listing without scrolling past it. It's page filler standing in for 1,529 real, live houses the stat bar just told me exist.
rows.beats: Redfin/Zillow's Central Oregon buy pages — this page wins on sourcing transparency (dated MLS citation, inline 'how we calculate this'), but loses on interactivity: their results are live, filterable, and browsable within the first viewport, while this page shows one motionless photo and a button.
rows.verdict: This is a correct, on-brand hero (Amboqia headline, navy scrim on the right mountain photo, sourced stats) sitting on top of a page that has no interaction anywhere in the first viewport and no catalog control installed — demoMatch is false because there is no shadcn-carousel, no inventory rail, nothing recognizable as a demo interaction at all. The stat bar edges toward the banned KPI-grid tell despite its plain-language framing, and the photo beneath it directly violates the Field layout lock by showing one static image instead of a scrollable field of live homes. Ship the carousel before this page can be called Field-compliant.

tells: "KPI grids" — borderline: the 5.0 Google Reviews stat is a bare number with a small "how we calculate this" link but no plain sentence telling the reader what 5.0 actually means (e.g. review count, recency).

defects.finding: Brief beat 2 (street address 115 NW Oregon Ave #2 on the fold) is missing — the left column names the six service-area towns but no street address appears anywhere in either screenshot, so a visitor cannot find the office without scrolling or clicking through.

All four form fields are static outlined boxes with no visible affordance beyond a hairline border — no focus state, no error state, no success check caught in either shot. It reads as a generic HTML form wearing house colors rather than a control that rewards interaction.

defects.section: TEXT / EMAIL / SCHEDULE row beneath the Call block
defects.finding: The three secondary reach options are reduced to plain column labels with no icon, description, or visual weight of their own, so the reach control reads as one strong Call block plus three afterthought labels rather than four coequal channels — flat originality, no section shape distinct from the form beside it.

rows.dullest: The TEXT / EMAIL / SCHEDULE row at the base of the left column — three plain uppercase labels with no visual encoding, cut off before any content renders, sitting directly below the one genuinely strong element on the page (the oversized CALL number). It's the exact point where the page's energy drops to a stacked-section default.
rows.beats: Beats a typical brokerage locator/contact page (e.g. a Windermere or Coldwell Banker "contact us" page, which is usually a static phone number and a bare form) on trust transparency — the live "Open now, until 5:00 pm" status and the sourced 5.0 Google Reviews stat with a visible calculation link are both things most competitor contact pages don't show at all.
rows.verdict: This is a correct, on-brand, functionally complete contact page — one clear ask, sourced trust stats, a working write path with SMS consent — but it is not visually breathtaking and demoMatch is false: the form fields are static cream boxes with no catalog interaction (no beui-input shake/check) rather than a genuine demo object. The missing street address on the fold is a hard competitive-brief miss (beat 2), and the TEXT/EMAIL/SCHEDULE row is a flat, undifferentiated stack next to the one strong Call block. It should look and feel like the Call block does — bold, sourced, alive — across every reach option and the form itself, not just the phone number.

tells: "KPI grids" — the "28 for sale · 3 pending" line is two colored-dot stats sitting beside plain prose with no chart, bar, or sparkline encoding them; it reads as a fact dump rather than a display.

defects.section: Houses/Land toggle + listings feed (right column, desktop; stacked, mobile)
defects.finding: The Houses/Land control is a flat two-button navy/cream group and the feed below it is one static card — no combobox, no filtering motion, no masonry reflow. Nothing here promises the visitor an interaction; it looks and behaves like a portal filter chip, not a catalog control.

defects.section: New-listings count and per-community stat dots
defects.finding: "1 house came on the market" and "28 for sale / 3 pending" are static digits with no motion cue. A live-count component would signal freshness (this page's actual advantage over a static competitor site) instead of reading like plain body copy.

On the 375x812 first viewport the alert copy ("Every new listing, by email...") is visible but the email input and submit button fall below the fold — the map above it consumes too much vertical space on mobile, so the layout-lock requirement that alerts sit in the first viewport is not actually met on the phone size.

Months of supply is required as two named bars per the layout lock, and no such module appears anywhere in either captured viewport — the page opens and stays on inventory count and a single listing card with no market-supply comparison visible.

rows.dullest: The right-column listings module: one static card, a plain two-button toggle, and a plain-text email form. It is the exact shape of a stock IDX widget — nothing here differs from what any MLS-fed template would render for any subdivision in the country.
rows.beats: tetherow.com (the community's own site) has no live MLS feed at all — this page wins on listing freshness and price data (a house-specific, dated, sourced $2.5M/4bd figure updating from MLS) that Tetherow's own marketing site cannot show. But it does not beat a strong portal place page on interactivity: Redfin's neighborhood pages already give scrubbable price-history charts and filterable map pins, which this page does not yet do.
rows.verdict: This is a correct, on-brand, quiet page — navy/cream, Amboqia headline, a genuinely useful custom boundary map instead of a generic Google embed — but demoMatch is false: there is no catalog interaction anywhere in the fold, just a static button toggle and one listing card. The stat dots and listing count are inert numbers that could be alive, months-of-supply is missing entirely from what's visible, and mobile buries the alert form's actual input below the viewport. It reads as informative and honest, not breathtaking or interactive.

tells: "Missing states." — the first viewport shows only static MOS bars and a static email form; there is no Atlas map or any element that responds to a hover, tap, or scrub anywhere above the fold.

defects.finding: The layout lock requires a place page to open with a drawing (Atlas) plus a figure beside the alerts sentence. There is no map anywhere in the first viewport on desktop or mobile — only the hero photo and the two static MOS bars. This is a required-section miss, not a style note.

The three new-listing results are a plain three-up row of tiny thumbnail + price + address, no card hover, no scroll behavior, no way to see more than three without leaving the page. It is a shrunk version of a portal results list, not a distinct display.

rows.dullest: The MOS bars and the new-listings row are both static, source-labeled facts with zero motion or response to touch — correct and honestly sourced, but nothing on the page moves, scrubs, or reveals more when touched, so the whole first viewport reads as a well-typeset printout rather than a living instrument.
rows.beats: Redfin's Awbrey Butte neighborhood page — this page wins on source transparency (an explicit 'Oregon Data Share' citation and an expandable 'how we calculate this' disclosure that Redfin never shows), but Redfin's own neighborhood page opens with an interactive boundary map with pins, which this page is missing entirely in the first viewport.
rows.verdict: This is a clean, correctly-branded, honestly-sourced neighborhood summary that is missing its required map and has no interactive layer anywhere above the fold — demoMatch is false because none of the catalog jobs on the option list (scrubber insights, live digit counts, combobox, masonry) show up; what's here is house-built static bars and a shrunk listing row. It clears the honesty bar and most of the craft bar, but fails the layout lock (no Atlas) and scores low on interaction and originality: a visitor sees numbers and a form, not something to touch.

defects.finding: The hero is a straight navy-scrim-over-photo-plus-headline treatment with no motion, parallax, or data layer — it reads as a template hero rather than something a visitor would screenshot, even though the office-exterior choice itself is correct per the layout lock.

rows.dullest: The reviews section: a 5.0 stat, five static stars, and a small grid of quote boxes with no hover, no carousel, no way to see more than the four shown — the exact 'wall of proof, not a proof experience' problem the rubric penalizes under interaction.
rows.beats: No win named — nothing in either viewport (no interaction, no carousel, no data encoding beyond a star rating) demonstrably outperforms a standard brokerage about page or portal agent profile on any named metric.
rows.verdict: This is a correct, on-brand opener — AboutFirm hero with office exterior and one purpose line, followed by V3Proof reviews — which respects the layout lock and avoids the three-broker-card opener failure. But demoMatch is false: no catalog interaction (avatar group, button group, carousel) is visible anywhere in either shot, and competitiveBriefPass is false because only beats 1 and 2 (firm story, reviews) are visible in the given first-viewport screenshots — closings, the Call/Text/Email/Schedule reach control, the team teaser, and the inquiry door are all below the fold and unverifiable here. What is visible is static: a photo hero and a list of quote cards, with the one truncated review card as an added craft defect.

defects.section: Homes for sale vs a month of sales instrument
defects.finding: The page's only data element is a snapshot two-bar comparison (1,529 vs 326.5) with no long-view trend chart anywhere on the page, even though the layout lock calls for a house-chart long-view series alongside the months-of-supply bars — a visitor has no way to see whether 4.7 months is rising, falling, or seasonal, only a single point in time.

Immediately after the one bar-chart section the page collapses to a plain-text 'Supply by property type, sale pace, and what the houses have +' accordion trigger and then jumps to a single-row 'More reports' list, leaving most of the visible viewport as bare cream whitespace on both desktop and mobile — this reads as an unfinished stub, not a comprehensive market report.

The two bars render as flat navy lines with a static dot at the value end; nothing in the shot (no cursor state, tick marks, threshold band for 'balanced', or scrub handle) signals that hovering or dragging reveals more data, so the instrument reads as a decorative illustration of two numbers rather than an interactive comparison.

rows.dullest: Everything below the hero headline and the one two-bar comparison: on both desktop and mobile the page is mostly cream whitespace bracketed by a collapsed accordion and a one-row 'More reports' link — there is no second data section, no chart, no animated figure, nothing to scroll for.
rows.beats: No win named — a Redfin or Zillow local market page, or the resort's own site, both show a historical trend line and multiple cut breakdowns (property type, price band, DOM) rendered by default; this page shows one live snapshot metric and hides the rest behind a '+' with no visible expanded content.
rows.verdict: This is a correct, on-brand stub, not a market report: the two-bar months-of-supply instrument follows the house-mos spec and the sourcing line is honest, but demoMatch is false because none of the prescribed catalog forms (house-chart, beautifului-insight, beui-number) are present anywhere in the shots. The page is dominated by empty cream space with a single static-looking data point and a one-line 'More reports' list, which is the opposite of the 'breathtaking, interactive on every page' bar — there is no trend, no scrubber, no live count, nothing that rewards a second look.

tells: "Not a Google default map" — a Google attribution wordmark is visible bottom-left on the desktop map. Even with restyled grayscale roads and navy cluster pins, the presence of the Google mark means the underlying tiles are Google Maps, not the site's own Atlas/TIGER cartography the layout lock requires.

defects.section: map panel (desktop split view, mobile map)
defects.finding: Google Maps attribution wordmark is visible, indicating this is a restyled Google Maps embed rather than the house Atlas (TIGER) basemap the layout lock mandates for search. Restyling colors on top of Google tiles is not the same system as the standalone cartography used elsewhere on the site.

The search input is a static labeled field with no visible morph/expand behavior, and the price slider fill reads as flat dark gray rather than navy with tick-stop motion — neither shot shows the field opening into results or the slider snapping to ticks, so the required catalog interactions cannot be confirmed as present.

The composition (dual-handle price slider with dot ticks, cluster-bubble map, plain photo+price+specs list rows, Map/Split/List toggle) is a near 1:1 reprise of Zillow/Redfin's own search page with no Ryan Realty-specific move — nothing here a template wouldn't already produce.

defects.section: mobile bottom bar (Saved Areas / Map-List-Sort / listing count strip)
defects.finding: At 375px, the Saved Areas button, the Map/List/Sort segmented control, and the "Homes for sale · 500 on this map · $57K-$6.6M" summary strip are all crowded into the last ~90px of the viewport with no visible spacing hierarchy between them, reading as three competing bottom-anchored elements rather than one coherent control bar.

rows.dullest: The whole search surface is the dullest part: a price-range slider with dot ticks, a cluster-bubble map, and a plain photo/price/spec list is exactly what every major portal already ships. Nothing here signals Ryan Realty specifically — swap the logo and this is Zillow.
rows.beats: No win named
rows.verdict: This is a competent, on-brand implementation of the standard portal search pattern (list + map split, price slider, cluster map) but not a page that beats Zillow or Redfin on any visible metric, and demoMatch is false because neither shot shows the search field morphing, the range slider snapping with navy fill, or the filter sheet opening — only rest-fold states were captured. The Google attribution mark on the map is a concrete signal the search map may still be riding Google Maps tiles rather than the house Atlas basemap the layout lock requires. Craft is solid (aligned figures, sourced stat line, tabular numbers) but originality is close to zero — this is the template, not a deliberate departure from it.

defects.finding: The layout lock calls for house-sheet: address, then a sourced answer, then contact, one question at a time on mobile. What ships is a single static card — generic Bend-wide stats (2,064 closed, $760K median, 633 vs 175 supply bars) sitting next to a bare address input and a submit button, with no address-to-answer reveal step at all. Nothing here is personalized to what the visitor types, and the address field itself is a plain bordered box with no icon, no InputGroup affix, no visible error/success state — it does not read as any specific catalog demo, just a generic HTML input in house colors.

The homes-for-sale-vs-a-month-of-sales bar pair is rendered as two static filled bars with end labels; there is no cursor, tooltip, scrub handle, or any other affordance suggesting it responds to hover or tap. It functions as a decorative graphic printed once, not a data section that rewards interaction.

Photo hero with a headline, followed by a floating card split into stats-left / form-right, is the same 'get your home value' template every national portal (Redfin, Opendoor, Zillow) already runs. Nothing in the composition, type treatment, or data presentation would let a viewer distinguish this from a generic seller-lead-gen template if the logo were cropped out.

rows.dullest: The months-of-supply bar block: two static gray/navy bars with numbers next to them, showing city-wide aggregate stats that have nothing to do with the address the visitor is about to type — it reads as filler placed above the fold rather than an answer.
rows.beats: No win named
rows.verdict: This is a competent, on-brand seller landing page — clean type, real numbers, working hierarchy — but it is not the house-sheet the layout lock calls for and demoMatch is false: there's no address-then-answer-then-contact progression, and the address field shows none of the InputGroup/Field/beUI-input affordances it's supposed to carry. The composition (photo hero + split stat/CTA card) is the same shape as every national portal's seller LP, the bar chart is inert, and nothing here would make a visitor stop scrolling or screenshot the page. It is safe and dull rather than breathtaking.

tells: "Scrolling lists as the design" — the Photographed Listings section is a stacked row list (thumbnail, address, price, beds/baths/sqft) with 18 rows and no visual encoding beyond a small photo; a table wearing hairlines, not a rail.

defects.finding: Listings render as a plain vertical row list instead of the mandated rail. The layout lock names shadcn-carousel adapted into V3Carousel for photographed listings, but the shots show sortable rows (Newest/Price Low/Price High/Most Beds) stacked top to bottom with no card/rail treatment — the exact list-as-design tell the rubric bans, and a direct miss against the route's own house-primitive requirement.

defects.section: Map legend (Fewer sales / More sales gradient)
defects.finding: The four-swatch gradient legend claims to encode '90-day sales density' but no corresponding shading is visible anywhere on the map itself in either screenshot — the dots are uniform gray with no visible density fill tied to the legend, so the legend reads as decoration rather than a working key.

rows.dullest: The Photographed Listings feed: 18 identical rows of thumbnail + address + price + stats, stacked top to bottom with sort tabs as the only interaction. It is correct and legible but it is a list, not a page — nothing here would make a visitor stop scrolling.
rows.beats: Tetherow's own community site (tetherow.com) — that page has no live inventory at all, so this page wins on real-time listing depth (18 active homes, price range, per-listing photos) tied to an actual parcel-boundary map. It does not beat a Redfin/Zillow neighborhood page on interaction or presentation — those also have image galleries and map-synced hover states this page lacks.
rows.verdict: This is a correct, on-brand utility page — H1, claim sentence with count and price band, sourced timestamp, and Atlas showing the true Tetherow boundary with per-listing dots and a price slider — but the Photographed Listings section ignores the carousel lock entirely and ships a plain scrolling row list instead (demoMatch: false). The map's density legend also has no visible corresponding encoding on the map, undercutting honesty/function. It reads as functional inventory, not a page built to beat a portal's neighborhood search.

defects.finding: The entire first fold on both desktop and mobile is type and two thin bars — no photograph, map teaser, or illustrative figure. For a page whose job is to sell 'Central Oregon cities,' there is nothing Central Oregon about it visually; it reads as a spreadsheet in serif type, not a place.

defects.section: overlay control ('OVERLAY A CITY AGAINST THE REGION')
defects.finding: Copy promises an interactive city-vs-region overlay and 'hover, tap or tab a bar for what it counts,' but nothing in either screenshot shows an actual control (no select chevron, no combobox affordance, no visible city list) — the interaction is asserted in prose, not demonstrated as a UI element, and no *-open shot was captured to verify it.

The two bars ('For sale right now' / 'Under contract in a month') and the seller/balanced/buyer scale beneath are correct and on-brand but visually identical in weight and color to any generic stat-bar component — nothing here would make a viewer stop scrolling or screenshot the section.

rows.dullest: The whole visible fold — hero line, one bold sentence, two navy/gray bars, one dot scale — is monochrome stat furniture. It's accurate and legible, but it's the floor for a data page, not a page that beats a competitor's city hub on delight.
rows.beats: Zillow/Redfin city hubs: this page wins on showing its own months-of-supply computation with a labeled seller/balanced/buyer threshold and a 'how we calculate this' source disclosure — something neither portal exposes at all. No win named on visual appeal or interactivity, since neither is demonstrated in the shots.
rows.verdict: This is a clean, correctly-sourced, on-brand stat card, not yet a breathtaking place page — demoMatch is false because no catalog interaction (combobox, carousel, insight cards) is visible anywhere in the fold, only prose promising one. The house-mos bars are executed properly, but the total absence of imagery, a map, or any city-specific visual in the first viewport leaves the page feeling like a spreadsheet with a nice typeface rather than a hub for 15 real places.

defects.section: stat bar list (597 lots / 59 commercial / 45 2-4 unit / 40 farms)
defects.finding: Four rows of number+label with a static thin bar underneath show part-to-whole composition but nothing in the shot promises a hover, tap, or scrub for per-type detail (median price, price range, freshest close date) — no cursor affordance, no tooltip state, no visible control at all in the first viewport, and no catalog component (shadcn table, beautifului scrubber) appears anywhere on the page.

The right-column paragraph plus 'how we calculate this' disclosure is honest and well-sourced but purely static text; the whole first viewport is a headline, a static bar list, and a paragraph — no data-journalism interactive layer anywhere above the fold.

rows.dullest: The four-row bar list (597 lots, 59 commercial, 45 2-4 unit, 40 farms) — a styled KPI list with a decorative bar underneath each row, nothing to touch, nothing that changes.
rows.beats: Beats a Zillow/LoopNet land search page on transparency — the cited source line and 'how we calculate this' disclosure is something portal aggregate counts never show — but loses badly on interactivity: those pages let you filter and sort live, this page is a static image of four numbers.
rows.verdict: This is a well-typeset claim-first headline over a static stat list, not the interactive data page the brief calls for. demoMatch is false — no catalog control (table, scrubber, carousel) is visible anywhere in the first viewport, house or catalog. The bars encode part-to-whole cleanly and the sourcing is honest, but nothing here rewards a hover or tap, which is the single biggest gap against both the rubric's interaction criterion and the assigned house-ledger/beautifului-insight jobs.

tells: "Walls of text." — the two intro paragraphs beneath the hero ("What Awbrey Glen homes sold for..." / "Awbrey Glen sits on Awbrey Butte...") run as unbroken prose with no figure, image break, or data callout sitting beside them despite the article being about a specific price and HOA number.

defects.section: Intro body copy, left column below the hero
defects.finding: Two full paragraphs of plain prose open the article with zero visual encoding — no pull quote, inline stat, or image break — even though the headline itself is built entirely from two numbers ($1,349,000 median, $87 HOA). The strongest material in the piece is stated, not shown, right where the reader's attention is highest.

The sidebar promises sourced numbers with sample size and window but renders only a static price and a flat one-pixel dash under it in the visible fold — no sparkline, no trend mark, no interactive way to see the other numbers in the guide without scrolling past the article. It's a KPI label dressed as data journalism with no chart backing it in view.

rows.dullest: The two intro paragraphs — a strong claim-first headline and a real drone hero photo lead into flat, undifferentiated prose with no visual break, right when the page has the most attention.
rows.beats: Most portal neighborhood write-ups (Zillow/Redfin style guides) publish a number with no provenance; this page's sidebar promise of window + sample size per figure is a real honesty win over that competitive set. But against beautifului.dev-style data journalism or the portal's own place pages, it has no chart, no interaction, and no visual encoding of the number it's built around, so it does not beat those on data presentation.
rows.verdict: This is a correct, on-brand article shell — strong hero, claim-first headline, an honest sourcing gesture in the sidebar — but nothing in the visible fold moves, scrubs, or reveals more on interaction, so demoMatch is false: there's no catalog control here at all, just static text and one static number. The intro reads as filler prose ahead of the numbers it's promising, which is the walls-of-text tell, and the sidebar's own stat card has no chart behind it despite the article naming a specific price and HOA figure. Fix is to put the numbers guide behind an actual beautifului-insight chart and treat the opening claim as a Quiet callout instead of two paragraphs of prose.

tells: "Missing states." — the desktop map renders a large blank quadrant (right half of the map box) with no plat detail or polygons, and the price-scrubber/zoom-control interaction visible on desktop is entirely absent from the mobile first viewport, leaving mobile with a static, non-interactive map thumbnail.

defects.section: the Atlas map ("Ridge at Eagle Crest right now")
defects.finding: On desktop the map canvas is roughly half empty — the right portion shows only faint unlabeled road lines with no subdivision polygon or data, wasting the hero interactive moment the layout lock calls for.

The price-drag scrubber, zoom controls, and House-type checkbox that make the desktop map interactive do not appear anywhere in the mobile 375px first viewport — mobile visitors see a static map thumbnail with no filtering affordance at all, so the page's one real interaction does not reach half its traffic.

defects.section: right column (new listings + email capture + two CTAs)
defects.finding: Crawlable links, one listing card, an email-capture box, and two buttons ("See every home for sale", "Talk to a broker") are stacked with almost no visual separation or hierarchy differentiating them — it reads as a generic lead-gen sidebar dump rather than one deliberate editorial moment.

rows.dullest: The right-column stack — a links list, one listing card, an email box, then two stacked buttons — is a generic real-estate lead-gen sidebar; strip the Ryan Realty logo and it would be indistinguishable from any brokerage's boilerplate neighborhood page.
rows.beats: Beats Zillow's neighborhood page on data specificity: Zillow shows a generic pin cluster over stock Google Maps tiles with no boundary awareness, while this page draws the actual plat polygons as a custom overlay and ties a live price-drag scrubber to that map — something no major portal offers at the subdivision level. It does not beat Zillow on completeness of interaction reach, since that scrubber disappears entirely on mobile.
rows.verdict: This is a page with one genuinely original idea — a hand-drawn plat-boundary map with a price-drag scrubber — bolted onto an otherwise stock real-estate sidebar of links, a listing card, an email box, and two CTAs. demoMatch is false: nothing here is a recognizable catalog demo interaction, restyled or otherwise, so there's no cream-box question, but there's also no borrowed craft from the shadcn/beUI bar to lean on. The map itself has an unfinished feel (a blank right half on desktop) and its one real interaction vanishes completely on mobile's first viewport, which is a functional regression, not just a taste one. It's competent and on-brand but not yet the page that beats every subdivision page on the internet.

tells: "Stacked-section page" — the right column runs the MOS card and the New Listings card back to back, both built as eyebrow → bold headline → rows/bars → source → 'how we calculate this' dropdown, with zero variation in form, width, or density between them.

defects.finding: Two consecutive sidebar cards share the identical eyebrow-headline-bars-source shape with no variation in form; the bars are flat static fills with no hover/scrub reveal, so the page's most data-dense real estate reads as a template rather than a designed instrument.

At 375px the +/- zoom buttons render in a separate white box that floats outside and to the right of the map's border, disconnected from the control it operates — reads as a layout bug, not an intentional affordance.

Every sourced number on the page is a static digit even though the page proudly cites live freshness ('as of Sep 12, 2026'); nothing signals the figure is live or just refreshed, so the honesty claim (freshness) isn't visually reinforced by any motion or state.

rows.dullest: The right-column stack — MOS bars, then the New Listings card — is two static panels with identical bones. Nothing there rewards a hover or a scrub; it would look the same lifted onto Zillow, Redfin, or any competitor's ZIP page.
rows.beats: Zillow's 97702 search page — this page's clipped-boundary dot-density Atlas map with house-type and price-scrubber filters shows real geographic precision Zillow's generic pin cluster doesn't attempt. But past the map, Zillow's list-and-map split view is more interactive than this page's static bars and single listing thumbnail, so the win doesn't extend down the page.
rows.verdict: This is a competent, on-brand data page — navy/cream held, sources cited per §0, the Atlas map is a genuine differentiator — but demoMatch is false: nothing on the page pulls from the catalog option list (no scrubbed insight, no live-swapping numbers, no combobox), it's built entirely from house forms. Past the map, the right column is the stacked-section tell verbatim: two identically-shaped static cards with a floating mobile zoom-control defect underneath. Correct and dull, not breathtaking.

tells: "Scrolling lists as the design" — the ALL PHOTOGRAPHED LISTINGS block below the carousel is a sortable list of thumbnail+address+price rows with no visual encoding beyond a tiny photo; on mobile it truncates to one row before the fold but the tab set (NEWEST/PRICE LOW/PRICE HIGH/MOST BEDS) signals it continues as a long list, which is a table wearing hairlines.

defects.finding: The sortable list rows repeat thumbnail+address+price with no data encoding (no price/sqft delta, no days-on-market, no bar or dot), which is the banned scrolling-list pattern sitting directly under a carousel that already shows the same 5 listings — redundant and undifferentiated.

defects.section: LISTINGS INSIDE THE BEND CITY LIMITS map
defects.finding: Every dot on the Atlas map renders identical size and color regardless of price or recency — the map communicates only density, not the price band the headline sentence just promised, so the map and the copy above it don't reinforce each other.

Cards show photo, price, address, beds/baths/sqft — identical to a stock Zillow/Redfin card with no Ryan Realty-specific insight (no price/sqft, no days-on-market, no momentum badge) so a viewer can't tell this apart from a portal card even though the carousel mechanics themselves match the demo.

rows.dullest: The ALL PHOTOGRAPHED LISTINGS list at the bottom — it repeats the same five listings already shown in the carousel above it, as a plain sortable row list with a thumbnail, which is exactly the 'wall of scrolling list' pattern Matt named as the standard to beat.
rows.beats: Zillow's Bend single-family search results page — this page names its source and pull time inline ('from the regional MLS through Oregon Data Share · read Sep 12, 2026, 4:44 PM'), which Zillow's equivalent page never states in the visible copy; that is the one concrete, verifiable win here.
rows.verdict: This is a functional, honestly-sourced place-type page with a working filter slider, a carousel that genuinely matches the shadcn demo interaction (visible arrows, visible card body, partial-cut cards on mobile), and a plain claim sentence instead of a KPI grid — demoMatch is true. But past the fold it collapses into the exact scrolling-list tell the rubric bans, the map dots carry no price encoding despite the page just promising a price band, and the listing cards are indistinguishable from a generic portal card. It is correct and on-brand but not breathtaking: a reader would not screenshot this to show someone.

defects.section: top stat row (median list price / homes for sale / under contract / days to offer)
defects.finding: Four static big-serif numbers with a caption sentence each — the sentence saves it from the literal KPI-grid tell, but nothing moves, nothing responds to hover or scroll, and it is the first thing on the page on both breakpoints. On mobile it is the ONLY thing visible in the first viewport, so the page's single interactive element (the price-history chart tooltip) never gets a chance to be seen before scroll.

defects.section: Homes for sale vs a month of sales (two-bar mos panel)
defects.finding: The two-bar months-of-supply comparison correctly avoids a KPI tile per the layout lock, but the bars themselves show no hover state, no value reveal on interaction, and no visual link to the adjacent chart's live tooltip behavior — it reads as a static illustration next to a genuinely interactive one.

The headline ('Bend housing market: a seller's market') is clipped at the very bottom edge of the 812px viewport, and the price chart with its working hover tooltip — the page's only interaction — sits entirely below the fold. A mobile visitor sees four numbers and a half-cut headline before any scroll.

rows.dullest: The top stat row: four large serif numbers over a one-line caption, repeated four times with identical form and no motion or interactive affordance — on mobile it's the entire first screen, so the page's one real piece of craft (the hoverable price-history chart with the Aug 2024/2025/2026 tooltip) is invisible until a visitor scrolls past it.
rows.beats: Redfin's Bend market-trends page — this page wins on sourced-figure transparency (an explicit 'SOURCE: Oregon Data Share MLS · as of Sep 12, 2026' line plus a 'how we calculate this' disclosure Redfin never shows), but it does not yet beat Redfin on data depth: no comparable-market filter, no multi-metric toggle, and only one interactive element on the whole visible page.
rows.verdict: This is a correct, honestly-sourced market page that follows the layout lock (two named mos bars, one hoverable long-view chart, one verdict with a trace) but stops short of breathtaking: demoMatch is false because no catalog control (beautifului-insight, beui-number) was actually installed — every number on the page is a static serif figure, not a live count or scrubbed insight. The stat row is dull by the rubric's own definition of dull — correct and on-brand, with no motion or interaction — and on mobile it eats the entire first viewport, burying the one section (the price chart tooltip) that actually rewards a hover. Fix the mobile fold order and animate the stat digits before calling this done.

tells: The three closing stat tiles (725 / 342 / $467,000) read like a KPI grid softened only by a caption sentence — same type size, same weight, no visual mark distinguishing 'all listings' from 'single-family' from 'price,' and on mobile they fall entirely below the fold of the first viewport.

defects.section: honesty banner ('We don't work in Medford')
defects.finding: The banner is a flat bordered rectangle with a left navy rule, a heading, a sentence, and a bordered button — it reads as a house callout box, not the shadcn Alert object (no icon, no rounded card, no visual distinction from a plain bordered div). The layout lock calls for adapting shadcn-alert into the house Quiet register, but what's on screen doesn't recognizably carry the demo's shape.

The dot-strip chart (address, bar, price) is the right form and beats a bare table, but the static shots show zero interactive affordance — no cursor, no hover state, no tap target styling, nothing signaling a visitor can scrub or tap a row for the listing photo/detail. As rendered it is a static illustration wearing a chart's clothes.

On the 375px viewport the three closing stats are pushed entirely below the visible fold — a visitor on mobile sees the honesty banner, the headline, and the chart, but never the inventory counts or median price without scrolling, so the page's strongest honest numbers are invisible on first paint on the device most visitors use.

rows.dullest: The stat-tile row at the bottom of desktop — three identical-weight number blocks with a caption line under each — is boilerplate MLS-stats-widget furniture. It avoids the literal KPI-grid tell only because a sentence sits under each number, but visually it's indistinguishable from any brokerage's stock 'market snapshot' component, and it doesn't even survive to the mobile fold.
rows.beats: Zillow's Medford, OR listings page — this page wins on honesty (it tells the visitor up front it's not the local market expert and offers a real handoff instead of pretending to be a Medford authority) and on showing the actual current asking-price spread as a single readable dot strip instead of burying it behind filters and a median-only banner. It does not win on interactivity, depth, or memorability — a portal's map and filter UI is more useful once a visitor is actually shopping Medford.
rows.verdict: This is a competent, honest out-of-market page: navy/cream identity holds, the dot-strip chart is a real step up from a bare table, and the copy doesn't overclaim expertise it doesn't have. But demoMatch is false — the honesty banner doesn't read as the shadcn Alert catalog object, just a bordered house callout — and nothing on the page rewards a hover, tap, or scrub, so interaction scores near zero. The mobile stat tiles falling below the fold and the flat, undifferentiated KPI-ish tile row keep this in 'correct and dull' territory rather than 'breathtaking.'

tells: "The stacked-section page." — the right column runs BEND RIGHT NOW / HOMES FOR SALE VS A MONTH OF SALES / NEW LISTINGS as three consecutive eyebrow → heading → rows → SOURCE blocks with identical card width, hairline rule, and no variation in density or media between them.

defects.finding: Three sections in a row (MOS bars, new-listings card, email capture) share the exact same eyebrow-caps-label + hairline-divider + SOURCE-footer shape with no change in width, density, or form — reads as one repeated card, not a designed sequence.

On the 375px shot the alert email form is cut mid-sentence at the very bottom of the first viewport ("Every new listing in Bend, by… Price" truncated) — the layout lock calls for alerts visible in the first viewport, not buried past the fold on mobile.

No catalog demo interaction is visible anywhere on the page — only the locked house forms (MOS bars, Atlas map, alert form) plus a plain slider, zoom buttons, and status tabs. None of beautifului-insight, beui-number, combobox, scroll-animation, or infinite-masonry appears, so the figures (633, 175, 121) sit as static text with no motion promised by any visible affordance.

defects.section: Homes for sale vs a month of sales bars
defects.finding: The two horizontal bars (633 / 175) are static fills with no visible hover, tooltip, or scrub affordance — correct as a form under the house-mos lock, but as shipped there is nothing here that rewards a visitor's attention beyond reading two numbers once.

rows.dullest: The right column: MOS bars, a single new-listing card, and an email box stacked as three near-identical cream cards with hairline rules — no motion, no hover payoff, nothing that isn't fully legible in the first half-second.
rows.beats: Redfin's Bend, OR market-overview page wins on presence (embedded charts, saved-search prompts everywhere) but never dates or sources a figure; this page's explicit 'Oregon Data Share · as of Sep 12 2026' citation on every stat and named row count (121 houses, 188 sales) is a real win on honesty/function. On interaction and visual distinctiveness, though, Redfin's page currently reads about the same as this one — no clear win named there.
rows.verdict: This is a clean, correctly-sourced, on-brand data page that follows its layout lock (Atlas map instead of a Google embed, MOS as bars instead of a KPI tile, alerts near the top) but demoMatch is false: no catalog interaction (insight cards, live-count digits, combobox, scroll-animation) is anywhere on the page, so every figure is static text. The right column repeats the same card shape three times in a row, which is the stacked-section tell, and on mobile the alert form is cut off below the first viewport. It should read as an editorial data page that rewards a hover or scrub on every stat; right now it reads as a correct but inert brochure of numbers.

defects.section: closings display (per broker, right of hero map)
defects.finding: Closings are shown only as a bare number ('7 closings in the last 12 months') plus a dot on the shared map. Brief 3 calls for past closings as house-row cards — photo, address, ClosePrice, beds/baths/sqft — in a carousel. None of that exists; the closing itself stays an abstraction, never a real sold property a visitor can look at.

defects.section: reach control (Call/Text/Email/Schedule row under each broker)
defects.finding: Call renders as a solid navy button while Text/Email/Schedule sit as bare underline-free text links of a different weight and size below it — four unrelated typographic objects, not one connected control. This is not the shadcn button-group demo (a single joined segmented control); it's a house rectangle plus loose links.

defects.section: page opener ('The brokers' + one-line intro, straight into Matt Ryan's row)
defects.finding: The fold goes from a two-line hero straight into the first broker's directory row (photo, title, license, stat, buttons) with no firm-story paragraph and no reviews section visible — brief 1 (firm story) and brief 2 (Google reviews door) are both absent from what a visitor sees before scrolling.

defects.section: broker portrait circles (Matt, Rebecca, Paul thumbnails)
defects.finding: Each broker gets one small static circular photo with no grouping, overlap, or hover affordance — a plain , not the shadcn Avatar/AvatarGroup object with its visible interaction model.

rows.dullest: The broker-by-broker row (small circular photo, name, title, license, a bare closings number, a button, three text links) repeated three times down the page — this is the same shape a hundred brokerage 'meet the agents' pages use, and it's the least original thing on the page even though the map beside it is not.
rows.beats: Typical brokerage roster pages (e.g. a Compass or Windermere agent grid) show zero transaction evidence — this page wins on data depth by pairing each broker with a live, MLS-sourced closing count and a geocoded map of where those closings actually happened. But it does not beat a strong 'meet the team' page on interactivity or photography, and it fails its own competitive brief (no firm story, no reviews, no closings-as-cards) badly enough that the win is narrow.
rows.verdict: This is a clean, correctly-branded broker directory — navy/cream, Amboqia display, tabular closing counts, a real geocoded map instead of a stock embed — but it is not the catalog UX bar: demoMatch is false because the reach row is a house button plus loose links rather than the shadcn button-group object, and the portraits are plain images rather than an Avatar/AvatarGroup interaction. Against the injected competitive brief it also opens as a broker-first directory with no firm story and no reviews in the fold, and closings never surface as the photo/address/price cards the brief specifies. The map-with-closings idea is the one genuinely original beat; everything else is a well-executed but generic roster list.

defects.finding: The address search is a plain static input with a placeholder and an 'F' shortcut chip. No open/expanded shot was captured, so there is no visible affordance that it morphs into results the way the beui-morphing-search demo does — as shipped it reads as a labeled cream field, which the rubric treats as demoMatch false by default.

defects.section: first viewport below the stats band
defects.finding: The layout lock requires live inventory visible in the first viewport, but the fold only shows three counted phrases (tour today / spoken for / closed) — no actual listing cards or rails are on screen before the scroll break into the 'one in five' narrative section.

defects.section: dot cluster beside the 'one in five under contract' headline
defects.finding: The scatter of navy dots next to the claim has no legend, axis, or label, so a visitor cannot tell what it encodes (geography? density? contract status?) — it reads as decoration standing in for data, which fails the honesty/function bar of every figure reading like it has a source.

rows.dullest: The navy stats band under the hero — three plain-English counts separated by dots. It's honestly framed, but it's still a static one-line KPI strip with no hover, sparkline, or breakdown behind any of the three numbers.
rows.beats: Zillow's Central Oregon search homepage — this page wins on freshness framing ('as of Sep 12, 2026' plus a sourced live-MLS line) and on leading with an editorial claim ('more than one in five listings already under contract') instead of a bare search box, but it does not yet win on inventory depth in the fold since no cards are visible before scroll.
rows.verdict: This is a real hero with a sourced, timestamped stat band and an editorial claim-first headline into a chart — a meaningful step up from a wall of text, and demoMatch is false only because no open-state shot proves the search actually morphs rather than sits as a static labeled field. The dot-cluster visualization is unlabeled and the live-inventory cards the layout lock requires in the first viewport aren't visible yet, so what's shown is a strong stats-and-claim opener that hasn't yet earned the interaction and inventory-depth wins the brief asks for.

defects.section: price-drop underline bar under each card's price
defects.finding: The navy sliver under the price is meant to encode drop magnitude but reads as a decorative underline — no scale, no tick, no comparison anchor, so a viewer can't tell -13.0% from -10.3% by looking at the bar alone; the number does all the work and the mark does none.

The caption promises 'smallest to deepest' ordering across 48 cuts but the chart is cut off at the fold with no visible axis label, tooltip, or hover-cursor state in either screenshot, so nothing in frame confirms it rewards a hover/scrub the way the copy implies.

rows.dullest: The four-up photo carousel — photo, dark price badge, price/was-price line, address, specs — is the exact card shape Zillow and Redfin already ship for a 'price cuts' filter. The drop-bar underline is the one attempt at differentiation and it's too faint to register as data.
rows.beats: Zillow/Redfin price-cut search results — this page wins on narrative framing (a plain sentence stating the median and deepest cut of the week) and on having a dedicated cross-listing severity chart at all, which portal price-drop grids don't show; neither competitor contextualizes the week's cuts as a distribution, they only badge each card in isolation.
rows.verdict: This is a real carousel with working prev/next controls and a card body that shows price, drop %, address and specs — not a cream box, so demoMatch holds. But the idea underneath is still a standard portal price-cut grid with one under-realized data mark (the drop bar) and a chart that's cut off before it can prove it's interactive. It clears the floor without beating it: correct, on-brand, competent, but the two things meant to carry originality and interaction — the bar and the dot chart — aren't legible enough in what's actually visible to earn their weight.

tells: "The stacked-section page" — hero (eyebrow/heading), then a two-card feature row (bars + chart, each eyebrow→figure→source), then a stat-pair row (number→label→sentence→source), then a CTA. Four blocks in a row with almost no variation in width, density, or media type.

defects.finding: The long-view price series is a house line chart with a manual year-pager and a bottom slider handle instead of the prescribed beautifului-insight paged-scrubber pattern — the option list calls for adapting that into V3Chart, and this looks like a from-scratch control instead, so there is no catalog interaction anywhere on the page (demoMatch: false).

The two-bar months-of-supply comparison is correct as a form (not a KPI tile) but reads static in the screenshot — no visible hover/tap affordance that would reveal the underlying counts or the threshold math behind '4.7 months' and the 'balanced' verdict.

defects.section: Median list price / under-contract stat row
defects.finding: Two static numbers with a one-sentence gloss underneath — functionally a KPI pair with prose bolted on. Both are sourced figures (list price, under-contract count) that would read as live data if they animated digits on load/update instead of sitting as flat text.

rows.dullest: The bottom stat-pair row ($749,500 median list price / 545 under contract now) — two flat numbers with a sentence each, sitting in the same visual register as the hero and the chart panel above it. It's the one place on the page where nothing moves, nothing can be hovered, and nothing distinguishes it from a template's 'stats' section.
rows.beats: Redfin's Central Oregon market-trends page — this page wins on source transparency (a dated MLS trace plus an explicit 'how we calculate this' link on both the supply figure and the price series, which Redfin never surfaces) and on a verdict that actually matches its own number (4.7 months read against a stated 4–6 balanced band). It does not clearly beat Redfin on interaction depth or property-type granularity.
rows.verdict: This is a correct, on-brand, quiet page — navy/cream, Amboqia headline, sourced figures, a verdict that matches its own threshold math — but it is not a catalog page: demoMatch is false because nothing on it is a recognizable shadcn/beautifului control, just a house line chart with a home-grown slider standing in for the prescribed beautifului-insight scrubber. Structurally it is the banned stacked-section pattern (hero → feature-card row → stat-pair row → CTA) with too little variation in form between blocks, and the bottom stat pair is the dullest spot on the page — a KPI pair in a sentence's clothing with no interaction promised. It should be the paged, scrubbable instrument the option list calls for, with the stat pair animating in as live counts, not a second static row under an already-static one.

defects.finding: At the bottom edge of the desktop fold, two large bare numbers appear with no visible label, unit context, or sentence explaining what they mean — reads as the start of a KPI-grid pattern rather than a continuation of the instrument's sourced, explained style set up above it.

The "2026  3/3" year pager and prev/next chevrons are small, low-contrast targets on both desktop and especially mobile (375px), with no visible affordance (no button outline, no hover/pressed state caught in frame) signaling they are tappable rather than a static label.

The page reads as headline, then a bar-comparison card, then a line chart — a competent but fairly conventional editorial stack; nothing in the visible fold is a choice a market-report template wouldn't already make on its own.

rows.dullest: The pair of unlabeled large numbers sitting at the very bottom of the desktop fold — no chart, no comparison, no sourcing visible in frame, just two big figures dropped in, which is the seed of a KPI-grid tell even though the rest of the page avoids that pattern.
rows.beats: A typical portal market page (Zillow/Redfin local market overview) ships a single static months-of-supply number tile with no history. This page wins on data depth and interactivity: the median-price chart carries a year pager, a hover tooltip resolving to an exact month/price, and a scrub slider, plus the months-of-supply verdict is shown as two named, sourced bars instead of one bare KPI number.
rows.verdict: This is a real instrument, not a KPI wall: the two named supply bars and the paged, hover-driven price chart are legitimate interaction and match the layout lock (demoMatch: true — nothing here is a catalog file cream-boxed into a navy rectangle). But the composition itself — headline, comparison card, line chart, then an unlabeled number pair trailing off the fold — is safe rather than distinctive, which is why originality lags design quality. Fix the small pager tap targets and give the trailing $750,000/30 figures a labeled home before they read as a KPI grid.

tells: "Cream box." — the four reviewer circles (MJ, EO, AH, DG) sit in a flat, non-overlapping navy row with a caption under each, not the shadcn AvatarGroup stack. No overlap, no hover-reveal overflow badge — it's a tab bar wearing avatar shapes, not the catalog demo.

defects.finding: The avatar circles are laid out side-by-side with labels beneath rather than overlapping/stacked with a hover-expand interaction, so the control reads as a plain segmented tab bar instead of the shadcn AvatarGroup object the brief names.

The x-axis ticks (2019, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026) skip 2020-2022 with no visual break or annotation, so a reader can't tell whether the axis is time-proportional or just year-buckets with data — the cadence of reviews over time, the one honest thing this chart could prove, is ambiguous.

rows.dullest: The avatar row itself: four identical filled-navy circles with two-letter initials and a name underneath. It's the one element here that any competitor's review widget already has (a reviewer photo strip) and being avatar-shaped instead of a plain button adds nothing since there's no overlap, no stacking, no reveal.
rows.beats: A typical agent-profile reviews tab (Zillow/Realtor.com static review-card list): this page wins on data depth by plotting all 25 reviews on a real timeline with year filters instead of an infinite scroll of cards, letting a visitor see review velocity and freshness at a glance rather than reading five cards deep.
rows.verdict: This is closer to right than most of the site — a big sourced rating, a full-text quote instead of a truncated snippet, and a genuinely original timeline scatter of all 25 reviews with year filtering beat the flat review-card list every competitor runs. But demoMatch is false: the reviewer avatar row imports the idea of an avatar control without the AvatarGroup stack/hover interaction the catalog demo defines, so it lands as a labeled tab bar in avatar clothing (the 'Cream box' tell). The timeline's skipped-year axis also leaves the one interesting claim on the page — review cadence over time — impossible to verify from the chart alone.
